Round 4009.decision_summary: Step T1 of L6 (tls on the cooperative engine). The trust policy is a parameter of the one secure channel, not a second channel: Pinned (the zid of the peer's key, decision D1, unchanged and still what an unconfigured session does) and Chain (the peer's certificate chain verifies against given roots). The library is built without a clock, so it checks no certificate date; the caller states the time (or none, for a device without a clock) and a verify hook holds every certificate of the chain to it. A name is checked only when the caller states one, which is pico's default. A server asks for a client chain only when given roots (mutual TLS). Key and signature types stay P-256 and ECDSA over SHA-256 until T4 and T5 read what real pico and zenohd certificates use.

Round 4012.decision_summary: Step T2 of L6. The dial and the accept of the secure channel under both policies, as the stream link's StreamDial and StreamListen, so the stream link runs over either unchanged. A chain stream offers NO credential zid: a router's zid is its own, not its key's, so the session takes the zid the peer states and the chain was the proof; a pinned stream is unchanged. The name a stream dial has is the address, so verify_name matches it against the IP SAN. A mutual policy missing its identity or roots is Unsupported and never connects. The listener never blocks on the network: one inbound handshake runs at a time (the arena holds one inbound session), each accept advances it, and a handshake that outlasts the deploy's clock budget, fails, or comes from a non-TLS or untrusted peer is dropped without failing the listener. The coop crate gains StreamListen for Box<L>.

Round 4022.decision_summary:
The host half of the parity program has a measurement that can be graded where it had none: the no-drop rate of the pico ABI against zenoh-pico (`scripts/host-bench/`, mode `nodrop` of `scripts/pico-compare.sh`). The upstream throughput examples send as fast as they can, and their control (pico on both sides) read "no samples", so no cell of them could be graded. The new publisher OFFERS a stated rate (a slot of one millisecond at a time), the subscriber counts what it is delivered, and the search (RFC 2544) doubles the rate and bisects to 5 percent: a rate stands when no put failed, every message was counted, the puts took at most 102 percent of the trial and at least 98 percent of the offered messages were put. The same two sources are built against zenoh-pico and against `libwz_capi_pico`.

A trial is valid only when the pinned CPUs were used by nothing else (the busy time of those CPUs less the CPU time of the two processes, over the CPU seconds the trial had, at most 10 percent; interrupt time is left out because the packets of a loopback stream are the test's own cost). This is what separates the hosts: on pc2, shared with other sessions' builds (load 15 to 30), every trial was disturbed and the unfiltered search read values tens of times apart between two repetitions of one condition, so none of its figures is kept; on pc3, which the owner said may be used freely, the three repetitions of every condition agree within 5 percent.

Measured on pc3 (TCP loopback peer, median of three, msg/s), with the puts batched per slot, which is how the upstream example reaches pico's best rate: 8 B at least 5.12 M for wz against 4.48 M for pico, 64 B 4.48 M against 4.00 M, 1 KiB 160 k against 310 k. With the puts one by one pico makes one `sendto` per put and reads 360 k at every size, and wz reads at least 5.12 M, 4.48 M and 190 k. So the pico ABI is ahead of pico by 12 to 14 percent on small messages in pico's best configuration, and BEHIND by half at 1 KiB. The round trip of the same ABI reads a tie at 10 to 11 microseconds. The wz figure at 8 B is a lower bound (the search stops at its cap).

A red of two other sessions' commits is paid in this round: `resource_budget_gate.py --check` failed on main since `b4a5d05f0b` and `97fb40d2a2` committed the stack chains of the FreeRTOS demo images `frt` and `frt2` in the stack gate, because the resource table must have a row for every committed chain and a row is a chain with a kit reading beside it, which a QEMU image has none of. The table now has a key `not_measured_on_the_kit` (image to reason) which the gate holds both ways (a declared image must have a committed chain, must not also have a row, and must give a reason); `frt` and `frt2` are declared in it. No row was invented for them.

The 1 KiB cell is a loss and its mechanism is read, not guessed: with one `sendto` per put on both sides, wz adds about two `futex` calls per put (298,725 calls for 150,000 puts against pico's 14), and 84 percent of its `sendto` calls are made by the writer thread and not by the thread that put. The zero-copy lend path (`OutboundTx::commit_at`) wakes the writer for every frame (`frame_landed`); the writer is asleep between two frames 20 microseconds apart; the sender-side flush that exists for a lone message (`flush_inline`, with its quiet-time and stream tests) is reached from the batch hook and not from this path. Writing a lone lent frame from the sender's thread by the same tests is the lever, and it is not attempted yet.

Round 4031.decision_summary:
Round 41 named the lever for the 1 KiB host cell: write a lone or large frame from the thread that put it, by the tests `flush_inline` already has. That was tried and measured, and it is not the lever. A frame that lands alone, or is 512 bytes or more, was written by its sender whenever the writer's role was free (`OutboundTx::send`, `send_reserved` and the pooled commit path), with the writer-queue tests (632 in the crate) and both clippy feature sets passing.

On pc3 it changed nothing: 1 KiB reads 155 k batched and 190 k one by one against 160 k and 190 k before, and 8 B and 64 B are unchanged (4.8 M and 4.48 M batched, 4.96 M and 4.48 M one by one). Per thread (`strace -f`, 1 KiB at 150,000 a second), 3 of 158,857 `sendto` calls came from the putting thread and the writer still took one `futex` pair per frame. By reading `recv_wire_tagged_with`, the writer takes the role together with a frame and keeps it until that frame is written, so at 190 k frames a second the role is almost never free to a sender. A sender that waited for the role is not safe: the writer can be waiting on the socket for the runtime thread the sender may be running on.

The change is not kept; the commit was dropped before any push. What is kept is the reading, in docs/upstream-parity.md, and the correction of the lever: the loss sits in the one-writer pipeline, so a fix has to shorten what the writer holds or take the hop out of the queue.

Round 4038.decision_summary: The observation round 4023 carried unexplained, a stock zenohd's admin listing losing its multicast locator after a mismatched member's datagram, is zenohd's own behavior and not a defect of wz. Upstream 1.10.2 returns an error from the receive task of a multicast link when a datagram does not decode (the batch fails to read, or the message does not decode) and then deletes the transport, so one such datagram from any member takes the group down for that zenohd. wz's receiver drops the datagram and goes on, which is the sturdier behavior and the one to keep: a member that disagrees about the compression wrap cannot end the group for the others. A comment of the receive path that said upstream also only drops a batch it cannot read was wrong and is corrected; the witness explains why its second member starts only after the first is listed.

Round 4042.decision_summary: A router told every face of a south region its peer hat serves (the peers of a group it is the gateway of) each subscriber and queryable that another region held, unasked, by a flood to the region's faces, by the face-up replay, and again by the answer to the face's interest: a peer that had asked for nothing registered a declaration for each, and one that asked registered it two or three times. Upstream's peer hat sends a face that is not north-bound a declaration of another hat only for an interest the face holds (`zenoh/src/net/routing/hat/peer/pubsub.rs` @ `fn maybe_propagate_subscriber`: the face is north-bound, or a remote interest of it matches), and does not repropagate subscribers to a new south-bound peer at all (`zenoh/src/net/routing/hat/peer/pubsub.rs` @ `New south-bound peer remote; not propagating subscribers`). The interest of such a face, subscribers and queryables alike, is kept in the interest store as push-reachable under a new role (PeerHat); what self advertises into that region goes to the faces whose interest matches, each at most once, and is retracted by id from the faces that were told it; the answer to the interest seeds what was said so that the push that follows does not say it again; the face-up replay of subscribers and queryables is not made to such a face; and a declaration that a peer of the region made is not pushed to another face of the region (its peers learn it over their own links, as the answer already withheld). Upstream's regions test, measured a process per test, goes from 64 to 78 of 126: scenario 6 putsub and getque, half of scenarios 3 and 7. Round 4047.decision_summary: Layer C0mut could not run on a build host, and the carry that called it a bx environment issue named the symptom and not the cause. The sweep starts its cargo child with `subprocess.run`, which closes every descriptor above 2, while the host's environment tells that child about a jobserver on descriptors 3 and 4 (MAKEFLAGS), so the child found nothing there; and the host puts sccache in front of rustc (RUSTC_WRAPPER) while the sweep builds incrementally on purpose (round 3140), which sccache refuses outright, so the baseline could not run `rustc -vV` and the sweep said the unmutated tree was not green. The sweep now builds its cargo child from `sweep_env`: no jobserver variables the child cannot reach, no compiler-cache wrapper it cannot use (a cache serves a crate compiled once from a clean tree, and this sweep recompiles one crate after a one-line edit a hundred times, which incremental state serves). Everything else of the caller's environment is kept. A selftest drives both directions: the variables are removed and nothing else is.

Round 4054.decision_summary: O4 (h), the Timestamp ZID bound, was reported to the SCE session and answered: the decode of a bounded length-ref field is meant to refuse a length past sce:max-size, because the largest encoded size of a codec is computed from that bound and a decode that accepts more produces a value that breaks it; the generator is wrong and the generated documentation is right. Only the C11 arm of the generator's length-ref decode compares the length with the bound; the Rust, C++, Kotlin, Go and Python arms and the string variant do not, and the same gap holds for sce:max-count on the heap-backed repeat decode and on the encode side. wz therefore adds no check of its own in a wrapper and does not change the generated documentation: the fix is the generator's and wz regenerates out/** when the SCE session says it landed. The item stays open until then; this round records the answer so the carry names what it waits for.

Round 4057.decision_summary:
The 1 KiB host cell of the pico ABI moved from about half of zenoh-pico's rate to 86 percent of it, by a change in how many frames one write of a stream's queue may carry. One by one, wz read 190 k msg/s against pico's 360 k; it reads 310 k (wz to wz, and wz to pico) against 360 k. Round 4031 named the lever wrongly: it said the writer's role and the hop to its thread were the cost, and that a fix had to shorten what the writer holds. The reading below replaces that.

Measured on pc3 (TCP loopback peer, 1 KiB at 150,000 a second, no strace). Counted inside the library, the role was held by the writer for 98 percent of the frames that landed and the writer was parked for 2.4 percent of them, so the futex calls that strace showed (298,725 against pico's 14) were in good part strace's own doing and the hop is not the cost. The writer thread spent 91 percent of its CPU in the kernel, in `sendto`, and it wrote exactly one frame per write (1,037 bytes on average). The write was bounded by the link's batch, 2,048 bytes against a pico peer, and two frames weigh 2,074. A batch bounds one FRAME; a stream carries frames back to back, so how many leave in one write is invisible to the peer.

The change: `write_bound` in `crates/wz-runtime-tokio/src/writer_queue.rs`. A write is bounded by the link's batch, or by four frames of the first frame's size up to 64 KiB, whichever is more. A frame small against the batch is bounded as it was (a test pins thirty frames of 100 bytes to the batch). With the bound widened to 64 KiB for every size, a probe at 250,000 a second made the writer carry 3.8 frames a write and keep up, and the no-drop search read 260 k; the rule that was kept reads 310 k and leaves small frames exactly as they were, because nothing measured says a wider write helps them and a wider write holds more of the lane while it is written.

Not the lever, measured: a frame written by the thread that put it whenever the writer's role is free. It changed nothing (190 k), and the counters give the reason: 98.2 percent of the attempts found the role held, 14,032 of 1,200,000 wrote. It was dropped before any push.

Two things that move the figure and are not the library, read and recorded: the default pinning gives a process one SMT pair, and wz's sender and writer are two busy threads on it where pico is one (with two physical cores the unchanged writer read 290 k); and the 64 B figure read 4.48 M in one session and 4.32 M in the next with the unmodified queue too, one step of the search, so a difference of that size between sessions is the host's.

Round 4061.decision_summary: Three things, one cause. Upstream's regions test counts, for each node, the registrations it makes of a subscriber or a queryable, and a member of a multicast group registered the declaration of every other member twice where a publisher was declared: once for the member's announcement of its subscriber on the group (MulticastTxItem::Declare) and once for its answer to the interest the publisher asks the group (the answer a zenoh-pico member needs, which wz keeps). The registries of what a peer declared (RemoteSubscriberRegistry, RemoteQueryableRegistry) now keep a peer's declarations as a set of keyexprs, as upstream's hat holds one registration per face and resource (`zenoh/src/net/routing/hat/peer/pubsub.rs` @ `fn register_subscriber`): a keyexpr the peer declares again, under the same id or another, is not news (a queryable's change of completeness still is); both rows are kept, so either id withdraws it and the matching watches read what they read; the application is told the keyexpr gone when the last declaration of it goes, under the id it was told it by. Nothing on the wire changes. The second is a regression of round 4042 that the E7 mesh test found (wz_router_hat_federates_data_across_two_routers, reported with its bisect by another session): a router now tells a south peer only what it asked for, and a peer node's own publisher asked nothing (declare_local_interest only recorded the interest for the admin legs), so the demo's --publish peer never learned that a subscriber existed beyond its router. A peer node now sends the interest of its publisher or querier (current and future) to each router it is linked to and a Final when it goes, and sends the stored ones to a router that comes up later, as upstream's peer hat does (`zenoh/src/net/routing/hat/peer/interests.rs` @ `fn repropagate_interests`); the demo's --publish declares one before any face registers; a router, which has no router to ask, sends none. Round 4067.decision_summary: Phase 5b of the router's task-per-face work: a request and a response are probed and held as a Push is, so they no longer park a face's thread on a full link and no longer pass the data their destination holds. Their value and payload may be a buffer of shared memory whose handoff the sender opens before the send, so the probe runs inside the sender's transaction, committed when the message left and dropped, giving back what it took, when it did not. The router holds one that finds no room only when it routes it on behalf of a face it can gate, when its QoS does not drop it and when it carries no shared-memory descriptor, since the relay maps such a buffer for its destination in a way a later send cannot undo; those keep the waiting send.

Round 4069.decision_summary:
The host table of the pico ABI gains the sizes between 64 B and 2 KiB, and the 2048 B cell is read. Up to 512 B wz is ahead of zenoh-pico (128 B: 2.64 M against 370 k msg/s; 256 B: 1.52 M against 370 k; 512 B: 680 k against 360 k), because one write of the stream's queue carries many frames where pico sends one per put. At 2048 B, a put past the 2,048 B batch (a chain of two fragments), wz read 125 k against pico's 185 k under the default pinning.

That deficit is placement, not the number of writes. Counted per thread under strace, pico makes two sendto calls a put (20,004 for 10,000 puts) and wz about one, the two fragments leaving in one write. At 120,000 a second wz's sender thread is 42 percent busy and its writer thread 86 percent, 82 percent of it in the kernel, and the default pinning puts both on one SMT pair. With the publisher given two physical cores, wz to wz reads 220 k against pico's 180 k (repetitions 220 k, 175 k, 220 k), so the cell is won when wz is given the CPUs its two threads need.

Two cells stay behind and are not explained by placement: 1 KiB (320 k wz to wz and 300 k wz to pico against 360 k) and 2048 B from wz to pico (160 k against 180 k). The common size of the gap, 11 to 17 percent, is a lead for the next reading, not a finding. No library code changed in this round.

Round 4071.decision_summary: The second link to a node is now refused while it is still being established, and no longer closed after it came up. Two peers that scout each other dial each other at once, and the two ends then admitted the link that completed first on their own side, exchanged declarations over it, and only when the rival came up closed the one the zid rule rejects (SharedSession::face_up in wz-capi-core, Admission::Replace). What crossed the closed link had been delivered to the application, and was delivered again over the kept one: the regions test of upstream read one registration too many for a queryable in about half the runs of scenario 6 (measured by tracing every link of a receiver: two links to the same remote zid, each told it once). Upstream decides at the handshake, the acceptor before it sends the OpenAck and the initiator before it sends the OpenSyn and again before it takes the OpenAck (`io/zenoh-transport/src/unicast/manager.rs` @ `init_transport_unicast`), so a refused link carries nothing in either direction. The node now does the same, as a collision is settled in BGP (RFC 4271 section 6.8) before the session is Established. A LinkAdmission (wz-session-core link_admission.rs) is installed on each link before its first wire byte and asked at three points of the handshake in the session core's drive.rs: the initiator at the InitAck, the acceptor at the OpenSyn, the initiator before the OpenAck is taken. A refusal sends Close(MaxLinks), the reason zenoh gives, and ends the open (DriverLoopOutcome::LinkRefused, OpenError::LinkRefused) with the FSM where it was, so the generated session machine is untouched. The node's table is LinkRegistry (wz-runtime-tokio link_registry.rs): a link already established keeps its place and a new one is refused, two links still in their handshakes that went the same way keep the first, and two that went opposite ways are decided by the zid rule that was already written (judge_second_link: the link the lower zid dialled is kept, the other is superseded and its initiator learns it before it declares anything). Only a link whose acceptor admitted it and whose initiator confirmed it carries a declaration, which the table's own test shows over every one of the 20 orders in which two crossed handshakes can interleave: exactly one link is up, never none and never two. The node that answers is the C API's peer (CApiForwarder, through FaceForwarder::link_admission, and the dial role's Dialer): its listener and its dials run in different loops over one registry, so only the registry sees the link another loop is bringing up. The router's own loop keeps its collision resolution, which decides after the link is up, and a loop that aggregates links (max_links above one) installs nothing. SharedSession::face_up still states the rule for a link that came up while no rival was known, and in the measured runs it was not needed once.

Round 4073.decision_summary: A router that hears of a peer from another peer before the peer's own entry reaches it kept an empty set of the peer's links for good, and two gateways of one region then both carried what only the primary should. The regions test of upstream (scenario 7: two routers and three peers to a region) read a sample twice at a subscriber in about a third of the runs of the five tests that show it (12 of 40). Traced by link and by verdict: the sample reached the subscriber from both gateways of its region, because the inter-region filter (`zenoh/src/net/routing/dispatcher/tables.rs` @ `impl InterRegionFilter<'_> {`) lets only the largest zid of the gateways a destination peer links to forward, and one router held none for that peer (gateways_of answered an empty list for the whole run, with the region's two gateways known) and the filter reads an empty list as "nothing to choose among, forward". The cause is the sn gate of the single-hop gossip ingest, which wz copies from upstream (`zenoh/src/net/protocol/network.rs` @ `fn process_singlehop_gossip_linkstate`): what a neighbour says of another node it knows is a zid and an sn and no links, and it sets the sn that the node's own entry, the only one that names its links, is later compared with; when the second-hand one arrives first (measured at the router: its first list from the peer read `new=0 updated=0` after a neighbour's list had already introduced the peer), the node's own entry carries the same sn and is dropped as not newer. Upstream has the same gate; its test runs on one worker thread, and here the order is the reading of how two handshakes interleave. The ingest now takes an entry of the SAME sn that names links when no entry of that sn has set the node's links yet (LinkstateNetwork keeps, for each node, the sn that last set them), which is no wider than it needs to be: the same sn is the same state, so what the entry adds is what a node that had heard it first would hold, and once the links are set the gate is upstream's again, so two nodes that announce each other do not do it forever (the same entry twice changes nothing, a test). An earlier form of the rule, for a node with no links at all, left the case of a node that holds the links of the sn before and hears of the next sn second-hand first (a router holding one gateway of a peer that links two was seen in an earlier trace); the rule keyed by the sn that set the links closes it. The residue is a different thing and is not closed here: a peer that links its second gateway raises its sn and tells the first gateway through a message of its own, and for the time that message takes the two gateways choose the primary among different sets (a router holding the peer's links as the first gateway alone, the other holding both), which is eventual consistency of the election and is upstream's too.

Round 4074.decision_summary:
The depth of the lane that the pico C ABI queues its frames on becomes a declared limit, PICO_TX_QUEUE_SIZE (Kconfig WZ_LIMIT_PICO_TX_QUEUE_SIZE), default 8; TxQueueConf::pico() reads it, clamped to upstream's 1..=16 for a queue size, and TxQueueConf::default() keeps upstream's 2. The 1 KiB and 2048 B cells of the host table, which stayed 11 to 17 percent behind zenoh-pico after round 4057, were bounded by this depth.

The reading: sampling the publisher at 1 KiB and 290,000 a second (150 stack samples under a debugger), the putting thread was in wait_for_room in 126 samples and the writer thread in epoll_wait in 148. A pico lane held two batches (4,096 bytes), so four 1 KiB frames filled it and the sender and the writer waited for each other after every four frames, bound by the wake latency of a futex and an eventfd. With the publisher on two physical cores, 1 KiB wz to wz and wz to pico read 320 k and 300 k at size 2, 540 k and 520 k at 4, 560 k and 960 k at 8, 560 k and 920 k at 16, against pico's 350 k to 360 k; 8 is the knee, so it is the default.

With the limit at 8 and the default pinning (one SMT pair), median of three on pc3: 1 KiB wz to wz 560 k, wz to pico 920 k, against 360 k; 2048 B wz to wz 230 k, wz to pico 480 k, against 180 k; 8 B and 64 B did not move (5.12 M and 4.48 M wz to wz, against 4.96 M and 4.32 M before, within one search step). Only the pico C ABI on the tokio engine reads the limit; the lwip and MCU paths use TxQueueConf::default() and are not touched.

The cost is stated and not hidden: wz spends about 27 percent more CPU than pico for the same rate (user time about five times), runs two threads where pico runs one, and a lane may now hold up to eight batches of heap while frames are queued. One host and loopback were measured, throughput only.

Round 4075.decision_summary: The acceptance criteria of the zenoh verdict, stated in groups. The thresholds are 2^-20 and a corpus cannot measure a rate that small: with no failure seen in n independent trials the 95% bound is about 3/n. Section 6.4 of the design note makes the claim in three layers: the theory (Ville) guarantees the nominal rate if the model is true and nothing tests it; the corpus tests the model at levels it can reach (2^-1 to 2^-10, the share of independent groups that cross each, with exact intervals) and the rate at 2^-20 is stated as an extrapolation; the cost is reported as expected sample size per group. Independence is counted in groups, the false no over zenoh groups and the false yes over null ones: claims of 10%, 5% and 1% need 29, 59 and 299 of each, and the corpus holds 22 and 18. A development corpus chooses the model; a validation corpus is collected after the model is frozen and fixed by a ledger entry before it is read. The levels are this session recommendation, not a ruling.

Round 4078.decision_summary:
Round 4074 stated that the wz side of the pico host table spends about 27 percent more CPU than zenoh-pico for the same rate, with about five times its user time. That statement is withdrawn: it was read from a run in which the publisher program spins between its 1 ms slots, a spin that is charged to the process and is long exactly when the library is faster than the offered rate, and the one wz reading was taken with a lane of two.

Read again with the spin replaced by a sleep (paced_pub -w), 1 KiB at 290,000 a second, a 4 s window of the per-thread ticks of /proc, lane at 8, two repetitions: pico's one thread 340 and 348 ticks of 400, wz's two threads together 231 and 236 (the sender 102 and 104, the writer 129 and 132). At that rate wz spends about a third less CPU than pico, mostly in the kernel, because it writes many frames in one call. Stack samples of the publisher agree: the writer thread was in epoll_wait in 194 of 200 samples, and the put path shows no single dominant function (memcpy is the top frame of none).

The split between user and kernel time is not stated: tick accounting put the writer's user time at 40 in one repetition and 0 in the other. The earlier claim that a vectored write or a zero-copy queue is the next lever is not supported by these readings and is dropped. The throughput figures of round 4074 are not affected: they come from the no-drop search, which does not use the sleep.

Round 4080.decision_summary: Step T3 of L6. The coop engine carries a session over a tls/ link, in both roles. The engine needed no change: it already takes a tls/ endpoint and is generic over SessionLinks. What was missing was the stack: IpLinks::open_listener answered a tls/ locator as unsupported, and it now opens the secure channel's listener (IpTlsListener, the tls/ twin of IpListener). The slot profile's acceptor is untouched because the engine is the heap profile's. Two decisions. (1) Two engines on two threads reach one library whose arena and key store are process-wide state with no lock, so a host-lock feature puts one mutex around every call into the C side, and each foreign declaration is both the function and its locked wrapper so a call added cannot skip the lock; an image that runs one thread leaves it off, and the lock is never held across a wait between calls. (2) The pinned zid binding is not a refusal at the handshake: the session reports it (peer_identity_verified) for the lifecycle verbs and the engine's port does not expose it, so T3 asserts what the engine can show and not a refusal that does not exist.

Round 4086.decision_summary: Step T4 of L6, first part: the PEM material a TLS config key names is resolved in one crate for both engines. The edge that holds the key spellings (pico's Z_CONFIG_TLS_*) resolves a file path or a base64 token once and hands PEM bytes inward, so no layer below it carries key-encoding knowledge; the cooperative engine reads the same keys as the tokio engine, and a reader each would write the refusal of an empty file and the trimming of a base64 token twice. read_pem_file and decode_base64_pem therefore leave wz-runtime-tokio's tls_config for a new crate, wz-tls-pem (std and the base64 decoder, no engine), and the tokio module re-exports them at the paths it has always had. The pico ABI now reads its keys through wz-tls-pem and not through the tokio re-export. The crate is a new one and not a module of wz-host-net because that crate's charter is what a hosted OS tells a node about its network. No behavior changes; the pico gate on transport-link-tls and transport-link-quic, and with it the engine-tokio selection, is unchanged and is the next part.

Round 4088.decision_summary: Round 4073's hosted run (41292703209, tip 9c61dbcb8c) was red in eleven jobs, and every cause was the link admission of round 4071, which is mine; a peer session read the run and offered to repair it, and was told it is mine. (1) The heap-free tests of the fixed-memory crates (C1bnl, C1m: session_pool_exhaustion, host_acceptor_fixed_e2e, session_slot_allocations) counted one allocation per accepted handshake, asked for by wz-session-core. The cause was found by the peer from the accept arm of the guard in drive.rs: it read the remote's zid with peer_zid(), which copies it into a Vec, for every OpenSyn whether or not the node guarded the link, so a build with a heap paid for a question nobody asked. The guard now asks the lease first (link_admitted_for_remote) and copies the zid of a guarded link to a stack buffer, so no build allocates for it; the three tests pass. This also corrects the reading in round 4071's verification, which put the lwip no-heap tests down as unreachable by heap-gated code: the gate was the heap feature of the crate, and those tests build with it. (2) tests/link_admission_mutual_dial_e2e.rs was gated on routing-accept and transport-link-tcp but calls peer_loop, which the feature routing-peer configures in (C1al, two jobs); it is gated on all three. (3) Two doc links named LinkAdmission, which exists only with the heap: the module doc of link_admission.rs (a build without it has no item to link, now a code span) and the reference definition for confirm in link_registry.rs (now the full path); the reduced-configuration docs of wz-session-core pass in 124 configurations and those of wz-runtime-tokio in 138 (layer C1bzr of each crate alone, unsharded; the hosted shards and their settle are the verdict). Round 4073's verification also said that no router held an empty set of a peer's gateways in the traced runs. That was wrong: of four traced failing runs two showed routers judging a sample toward a peer with an empty set while both gateways of its region were known, one of them both routers. The retained trace shows why: a peer sent the declarations of its subscribers to a router before the list of its links (SharedSession::face_up replayed the declarations and then sent the gossip), so the router knew the subscriber and not the node, and the inter-region filter read an empty set as nothing to choose among and forwarded from every gateway. The peer now sends the gossip first: the link is FIFO, so whoever learns a declaration of the node has already learned its links, which is also the order upstream sends them in (Gossip::add_link on the creation of the link, declarations after it). Regions scenario 7 then fails 2 of 120 runs, against 7 before this order and 23 before round 4073; scenario 6 passes 30 of 30. The order is held by a test that decodes the frames a new face is sent (a_new_face_is_sent_its_topology_before_any_declaration), whose control with the replay first fails reading declaration, topology.

Round 4091.decision_summary:
The cause given for the pico lane depth in round 4074 is corrected. It said that the sender and the writer wait for each other after every four frames, bound by the wake latency of a futex and an eventfd. Three temporary changes of the queue, measured at 1 KiB with the publisher on two physical cores (two repetitions each), read otherwise.

Waking a sender only when the lane is at most half full left size 2 where it was (wz to wz 315 k, wz to pico 300 k against 320 k and 300 k): the wake rule is not the cause. Counting only the frames still queued, and not the batch the writer is writing, took size 2 to 560 k wz to wz and 590 k wz to pico: the cause is single buffering. A lane of two batches is full while the writer writes one, so the sender has no room until the writer asks for the next batch and production and writing do not overlap. With the same accounting at the default size 8 the lane read 570 k and 940 k, what size 8 reads unchanged (560 k and 960 k). What size 2 lacks even with the accounting, 590 k against 960 k to pico, is room to queue ahead of the writer, so the depth is a gain of its own.

Nothing was applied: the accounting adds nothing to size 8, and it would move the memory bound of a lane from what it holds to what is queued plus the batch being written. The limit PICO_TX_QUEUE_SIZE stays at 8 and keeps its meaning. The mechanism and the three rows are recorded in docs/upstream-parity.md, and the statement of round 4074 on the cause is withdrawn.

Round 4096.decision_summary: Step T4 of L6, the ABI: pico's tls/ opens on the cooperative engine through the exported z_* symbols. Four moves. (1) The PEM a Z_CONFIG_TLS_* key names is read by one crate, wz-tls-pem, which the tokio engine re-exports at its old paths and the pico ABI calls directly: the edge that holds the key spellings resolves path or base64 once, and no engine carries key-encoding knowledge. (2) CapiTlsConfig, the resolved material, is the port's value and wz-capi-core re-exports it; the rule that a client pair is whole or absent is the port's. (3) wz-capi-coop's tls-mbedtls feature gives tls::HostTls, the dial and the listen of a host stack made from that material. The channel was built for an image, and a host program that opens sessions over its life has none of what an image fixes, so the provider settles three things: the library starts on an arena of its own on first use, an identity and a set of roots are made once for each distinct PEM and lent for the program, and the time of each dial and accept is stated to the roots through Trust::set_now, new in this step, so a certificate that lapsed while the program ran is refused at the next handshake and not accepted for as long as the program lives. A pico program dials with its connect_* pair and listens with its listen_* pair and the channel's policy holds one identity, so the value holds a dial for each role. (4) pico's tls-mbedtls feature resolves the keys, gives the stack HostTls and selects the cooperative engine. Features add and the engines add with them (engine-tokio on is the tokio engine, as engine-coop beside it always was), so the choice is not a compile_error: that was built first and removed, because it broke --all-features and the gates built on it.

Scenario 7 then failed 2 of 200 runs without a trace and 5 of 200 with one, the same rate as 2 of 120 before it, and a trace of the crossing decision in the first failing run (the others were not read) shows why it cannot help: the router that forwards a second time holds the peer's links as current (a set of one gateway, no hearsay of a newer sn), and the peer's second link is simply not yet told to it. Nothing in the protocol orders the two links, upstream has the same window, and closing it needs a hold or an acknowledgement the pin lacks. Round 4102.decision_summary: Step T4 of L6, the real programs: upstream's z_pub_tls and z_sub_tls run against the cooperative engine and pass in both directions, the two legs that Layer E skipped by name while the engine had no tls/ link. Measured, in order. The certificates those examples carry are RSA-2048 (a minica root, an end certificate signed sha256WithRSAEncryption, a PKCS#1 RSA PRIVATE KEY) and the channel's Mbed TLS built P-256 and ECDSA only, so both legs failed in z_open at once and the example says only "Unable to open session!". The crate's rsa feature gives the host RSA keys, RSA signatures read to verify a chain and RSA-PSS, and a 600 byte public key buffer in place of 160; it is the host's, the kit image configures the channel by Kconfig and never sets it, so the kit is unchanged, and wz-capi-coop's tls-mbedtls turns it on. With that both legs failed again, now in the handshake. OpenSSL, run against the same chain in both directions, named the cause: dialling got no suitable signature algorithm and accepting ended in alert 40. TLS 1.3 signs a handshake with an RSA key by RSA-PSS, and Mbed TLS's TLS layer lists rsa_pss_rsae_sha256 in its signature algorithms only when MBEDTLS_X509_RSASSA_PSS_SUPPORT is defined, which the crypto side's PSA_WANT_ALG_RSA_PSS does not do; that macro is in turn refused by Mbed TLS's own configuration check without PSA_WANT_ALG_RSA_OAEP, which the channel does not use and now carries for that reason. After it OpenSSL negotiated TLSv1.3 with TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256 and verified the chain both ways, and the two real-program legs pass. TLS 1.3 alone served upstream's examples as built (Mbed TLS 3.6.4 with 1.2 and 1.3 on, against a channel that speaks 1.3 only). Layer E and Layer Z, which build one artifact path, build the cooperative library with tls-mbedtls, the sweep no longer skips tls, and its count is 32.

Round 4107.decision_summary: The verbs of the admin node on Zephyr's sockets are witnessed through the query transport on the target. In deploy/zephyr-admin-loopback the fixed-memory client, which dials the admin node over tls/, now asks two GETs through its session: session/status/<peer> and session/close/<peer> under the node's zid. The status its key is listed for is answered with a status document, and the close it is not listed for is refused by name, so the zid the node decided by is the one the session's key proved and the plumbing of the requester (decision D12 step 1) carries it through a real session. The pair discriminates both ways: an unproven requester would be refused the status, and a node that took the requester for anyone would answer the close. A verb the build did not compile in is answered with nothing at all, not refused: the first build bound status alone and the close GET came back empty; the witness binds all four, as the product image does. What remains is D14's witness on the kit, with a real router's session reaching the verbs of the product image.

Round 4108.decision_summary: A consumer measured that a gap on a multicast group link is never counted: the passive reader set the SN ring only from an InitAck, so every Frame and Fragment of a UDP multicast or raweth flow read without_resolution. On a link with no handshake each sender's JOIN now states the ring its SNs are judged on (S clear states the defaults) and where they start: every conduit holds next_sn minus one, per priority under QoS, as upstream's receiver syncs a peer it learns. A later JOIN of the same sender moves nothing; one naming another zid, ring, role, lease or QoS starts the sender again. Rings are per direction, so two senders on one flow are judged apart. A JOIN on a link with a handshake is inadmissible and folds nothing. Field document 48 and census 22 record the moved values; no key moves.

Round 4110.decision_summary: Step T5 of L6: zenohd against the cooperative engine, both roles, over tcp and over tls/. Measured first on the tokio engine as the reference: a wz subscriber behind a real zenohd router hears a real pico put on tokio and did not on coop, with plain tcp too, so the fault was not TLS. A zenoh router names a subscriber's key in a push by an id the subscriber itself declared (the receiver's id space, mapping 0, a non-local wire expression). A peer publisher uses its own aliases (sender space) and was heard all along, which is why the earlier coop legs passed. The fix installs the link's actions as the own mapping space of the face's subscriber table when the link's wire is built, behind a wrapper that is Send and Sync on the same confinement argument as the rest of the engine. A first reading of this as an empty router route was wrong: it came from a log cut short by head; the full log shows the router computing a route with a subscriber to the coop face. Three legs now run on both engines in Layer Z: wz dials a zenohd tls listener, a plain tcp control, and zenohd dials a wz tls listener. The accept leg with wz as publisher failed on tokio as well and was replaced by the subscriber arrangement; the publisher direction through a router over tls/ is not covered. A separate red was found and fixed with it: for_each_record in wz-session-core was built for every codec-frame test build but called only under codec-push, so a build without codec-push failed its lib tests on a dead-code error, five run-ci guards at once; it is gated on the callers' cfg.

Round 4121.decision_summary: Round 4098 left regions scenario 7 failing 1 to 2.5 percent of runs on a repeated timestamp and named the cause as a window the protocol does not order: a peer that links a second gateway sends its declarations over the new link while its announcement of that link, sent over the first, is still in flight, so the first gateway still holds the peer's links as itself alone and both gateways elect themselves primary and carry one sample twice. That round left open whether to close the window with a hold or record it as upstream's own. This round closes it with a barrier, and the answer to the open question is that the window is closed, bounded, and costs the dialling side one round trip. A first experiment confirmed the cause before any design: holding the declaration replay of a dialled second link for a fixed 100 ms gave 0 failures in 600 runs against about 1.4 percent without it. The barrier replaces the fixed delay by what the delay stood for. A dialled link is announced first (the gossip send to every other face that hears of a link); then the dialling side asks each of those faces a liveliness get on a reserved key and waits for the final of the answer, which on a link that keeps order comes after the announcement was handled; only then are the declarations replayed over the new link, and a bound of 1000 ms ends the wait if a face never answers. The wait is an await, not a blocked thread: the first attempt blocked the drive thread and was wrong twice over, since the runtime refuses a blocking section on a local task set and, on the serial drive, the very tasks that read the answer run on the same thread. The accepting side keeps the unbarriered face_up, since it cannot await in its synchronous trait and the dialling side is the one whose announcement races its declarations. During the wait the face is already in the registry with empty tables and owes nothing yet; the first await version left it out and dropped the gossip sent to it, which failed 40 of 400 runs, ten times the baseline, and the replay then skips whatever the registry declared to the face in the meantime. Measured on a build machine through the suite tool with Z8_ONLY=scenario7:: and Z8_REPEAT: 1200 runs of scenario 7 failed 4 times (0.33 percent) against about 17 expected at 1.4 percent; 200 runs of scenario 6 all passed. The barrier does not reach zero: 2 of the 4 failures are the repeated timestamp and 2 are an equality assertion of a queque test whose cause is not attributed. Corrections to earlier entries arrive here, not in them: round 4098 said the window was closed only by an owner's hold; it is closed by an acknowledgement the family can ask for with its own liveliness get, no pin change.

Round 4122.decision_summary: The listener of Zephyr's sockets sets SO_REUSEADDR before it binds, as the POSIX listener does, so a node restarted on its port is not kept off it by the connection the earlier listener closed first. The witness is in deploy/zephyr-tls-loopback: a listener serves one connection, closes it first and goes, and a listener on the same port must bind at once. It discriminates: with the option applied the image prints that the restarted listener took the port and Layer Qz passes, with the option never applied the same image fails with a refused bind (Bind(-1)). Building the witness showed a second limit of the image that the product images will meet when they restart: Zephyr's TCP side of a context is a connection object from a pool of CONFIG_NET_MAX_CONN (4 on an IPv4-only build, not CONFIG_NET_MAX_CONTEXTS), a closed connection keeps its slot in TIME_WAIT, and a listen with no free object is refused (-1); the witness image states 16. The product admin image states CONFIG_NET_MAX_CONTEXTS only and keeps the default of 4 connections; whether a restart under load needs more is not measured and is not changed here.

Round 4128.decision_summary: L6 carry items after round 4112, measured, and one fixed: the host build of the secure channel held 7 sessions, not the 198 its arena takes. The publisher a router dials: a zenoh (Rust) peer publisher, listening and dialed by a real zenohd, reaches a pico z_sub client behind the router in 2.5 s, because it sends Interest(CurrentFuture, keyexprs and subscribers) for its publisher's key as soon as the link is up and the router answers by propagating the client's subscriber to it. The real pico z_pub and wz's pico drop-in z_pub send neither that Interest nor a Push to the router. That is pico's rule and the drop-in keeps it on purpose: a pico peer asks only while it holds a router as a peer at the time it declares, and here it declares before the router dials. It is therefore not a defect of wz's channel or of the drop-in's parity, and no test pins it, since a test of nothing delivered would hold wz to pico where wz may do better. Round 4112 said the suite has no built Rust example; that was wrong, scripts/build-zenohd.sh installs zenoh_z_pub beside zenohd. TLS 1.2: a client offering 1.2 only is refused with the protocol_version alert and the listener sees nothing to accept; the channel has 1.3 only by design. The arena against a count of sessions: a held server session takes about 20 KB with an RSA-2048 certificate and the 4 MiB arena takes 198 of them, but what bound a program first was the PSA key store, which the library sizes to 32 keys by default and an established session holds four of (7 sessions held, the eighth handshake dropped without a word, 4 MiB unused). The host build (feature host-lock) now sizes the store to 1024; the kit image sizes it by Kconfig and is untouched. The examples' certificates are valid from 2023 to 2123, so no leg depends on a date.

Round 4134.decision_summary:
The host throughput comparison is extended from the pico family to the zenoh-c family: the same publisher and subscriber sources are built against the zenoh-c 1.10.2 release and against wz-capi-c (scripts/pico-compare.sh nodrop-c, with one compatibility header for the two C APIs), and the 64 B and 1 KiB cells are recorded. The 8 B cells with wz in them are not stated: a measured loss at the end of a run, not the rate, stops them.

The loss was found by changing one thing at a time. A wz publisher dropped before its session loses the last 500 to 1100 puts in 4 to 16 of 20 runs at 400 k/s; left to the session drop, or after a pause of 5 ms, it loses none. Round 4141.decision_summary:
Upstream's liveliness test regression_1 failed on wz at 3599 (a subscriber got a sample before the token was undeclared) in 4 of 300 runs on a tree that also holds the control-frame fence, and in none of 105 without it. The fence only moved the timing; the race was already there.

Cause, read from the debug log of the failing runs: a peer node and the router node it joins keep their links through RouterForwarder, which did not implement FaceForwarder::link_admission. The default is None, so the handshake never asked the node whether a second link to a held node may carry anything. Two peers that dial each other (the configured endpoint on one side, the autoconnect of the gossip on the other) made three links; all three came up as faces, the first one replayed its declarations, and then the accept loop's decision after the link is up closed face 1 for the link the lower zid dialled. Closing face 1 retracted the token its peer had declared on it (the application was told a Delete) and the replacing face declared it again (a Put). Only the C ABI's own forwarder (CApiForwarder) answered the admission, which is why the registry and its twenty-order model test existed and the router nodes did not use them.

The repair is the textbook one for a connection collision (RFC 4271 section 6.8, and the handshake-time decision upstream makes in its transport manager): decide while the link is still being established. RouterForwarder now owns a LinkRegistry built from its own zid and answers link_admission with it, so an established link keeps its place, of two links still in their handshake the one the lower zid dialled wins, and the loser is closed with MaxLinks before either end declared anything over it. A face leaving releases its place at once (release_link_admission in deregister), as the C ABI's registry does, so a node that comes back is not refused for the link that left. The decision after the link is up stays for a link that came up while no rival was known and for a loop that aggregates links.

The loop-level test of two routers dialling each other asserted that the lower zid's link is always the one kept, which was what the decision after the link is up gave and is not what the handshake gives: a link that is already established keeps its place. It now asserts what matters to an application: one face each, the same link at both ends, and one FaceUp with no FaceDown at each node.

Round 4143.decision_summary: The carry item "how pico itself settles a certificate's dates" is answered by reading. In the pinned zenoh-pico, the TLS stream refuses a handshake whose verify result holds any flag outside a short ignore list: a name mismatch on a dial that did not ask for the name check, and a skipped verification on a listener without mutual TLS. Expired and not-yet-valid are not on it, so a lapsed certificate is refused, provided the platform's Mbed TLS reports dates at all: BADCERT_EXPIRED is set only under MBEDTLS_HAVE_TIME_DATE in the pinned Mbed TLS. The provider states the host's wall time at each dial and refuses a lapsed certificate (tls_provider), so the two agree on a host; a pico build without a clock checks no date, which is its platform's property and not a mode the provider offers.

Round 4147.decision_summary: The cooperative engine now decides a second link to a held node in the link's handshake, as the tokio nodes do, instead of after both ends have brought it up. The table behind the decision moved into wz-session-core (LinkBook, and LinkRegistry over the runtime's own lock) so that one table answers for every engine; the tokio registry is an alias of it. Each cooperative link takes a lease before its handshake runs, an established link keeps its place, and of two links still in their handshake the one the lower zid dialled is kept. The face swap after the handshake (admission, displace) is gone: the engine builds only where pointer atomics exist, so the branch for a target without them could not be compiled. The dial role's face that a node refused stands by until no other face reaches that node, read from the face table at each step, so a link that dies in its handshake frees the node as well.

Round 4148.decision_summary:
A session that closes while its data plane holds an open frame no longer drops that frame. Small puts are staged into the open frame of their priority and the link's writer puts it on the wire when it falls idle, through a hook that holds the session weakly; OpenedSession::drain_to_close let go of the session first, so a close that came before the writer's idle flush found the hook empty and the frame was dropped with the session. The puts of the last milliseconds of a burst had returned Z_OK and never arrived. drain_to_close now hands the open frames to the writer (batch_flush) before it lets go, and the seal that follows drains them.

This is a second cause beside the one recorded in the host comparison round. The undeclare of a dropped publisher is a Control barrier that already hands the open frame over, and then overtakes it on the writer lanes (the barrier in the lanes, landed since, holds it back). A close with no undeclare has no barrier, and the open frame was lost. The earlier statement that a close left to the session loses nothing was a reading of timing on that tree, not of the code, and is withdrawn.

Round 4151.decision_summary: The policy reply-auto-timestamp (G5 of the switch catalogue): what a queryable's reply carries when its handler gave it no timestamp. Upstream's reply builder holds only the time its caller gives (reply.rs, default None) and stamps puts alone (session.rs, new_timestamp); a node that wants its replies ordered by one clock had no way to say so. Off is upstream's. On, QueryResponder stamps its four plain reply forms (reply, keyed, delete, keyed delete) with the next stamp of a ReplyClock, which NodeHlc is, so a reply and a put of one node are ordered by one clock. A reply with its own time, an error, and the forms that are unstamped on purpose keep none. The host gives the clock to a queryable only when the policy is on and the queryable stamps.

Round 4160.decision_summary: The carry item "the drop counters of TlsListener are not reachable from the C ABI" is paid, and not with a new door. A C program has no listener handle, so an accessor would have had to be a process-wide count behind a new wz_ext symbol; the node already has a log that the library writes what it says about itself into (event-ring, library sources from 0xFF00), and a handshake the arena or the key store had no room for is what the node should say there. The host provider now keeps the typed listener (TlsDial::listen_counted) and, in a build with event-ring, writes one library event per drop: source 0xFF01, level 255, two integers, why (stalled, no room, other) and the channel's own code. Measured on the way: an arena that runs out is the channel's OutOfMemory, in the handshake with the RSA configuration and in starting the session without it (accept answers that one with an error, which TlsListener now counts as well); a key store with no free slot returns PSA's insufficient-memory code, which the channel maps to the same, read and not measured. The meaning of last_drop changed to the latest drop's own error, None for a stall, so that an event can say what it was. The zenoh-c ABI's header does not list the source: that ABI has no secure channel on this engine.

The peak is of the sessions the node can hold at once (SESSIONS is 2) and of the sequence the run drives; a build that holds more sessions, or a handshake pair in flight together, has its own peak, and the line says it.

Round 4165.decision_summary: The capability declarations-synced-event (G3 of the switch catalogue). A listener saw the peer's declarations as a stream with no mark where the peer's picture of itself ends and live changes begin, so a program could not read "no subscriber on this key" as "nobody wants it". The boundary is one wire message, the DeclareFinal of the initial interest, which ends the first burst of subscribers, queryables and tokens alike; so it is a fact of the peer, not of a plane. DeclEvent::Synced is delivered to a listener of any plane, once per establishment, by the host session reading the subscriber plane's flag before and after a dispatch. A listener declared after the peer finished is not told, because it was not given what came before: it reads Session::peer_declarations_final. Off, nothing is installed or fired.

Round 4169.decision_summary: The carry item "a key store with no free slot is read to map to the channel's out-of-memory and was not measured" is paid, and the reading was wrong. A new test binary (wz-tls-mbedtls tests/key_store_exhaustion.rs) starts an arena of 64 MiB so that the key store of the host build (1024 keys, four per held session) runs out before the arena does: 255 sessions are held, the 256th handshake is dropped and counted, and the arena's peak is 5.0 MB of the 64 MiB. The channel's error for that drop is Code(-0x6E00), Mbed TLS's generic handshake failure (MBEDTLS_ERR_SSL_HANDSHAKE_FAILURE), not OutOfMemory: Mbed TLS reports the PSA refusal from inside the handshake under its own code, so the channel never sees PSA's insufficient-memory code on that path. The code alone therefore does not name a full store (a refused peer gives the same one); the held count and the arena's peak do. The event log follows: NO_ROOM is the arena's, and a full key store is reported as OTHER with that code. The words in stream.rs, wz-capi-coop tls.rs, events.rs, event_log.rs, wz_ext.h and the design note that said the arena or the key store had no room for NO_ROOM were corrected to say the arena only. Round 4172.decision_summary: The capability remote-declaration-watch (G3 of the switch catalogue). A declaration listener is told what the peer declares, and a session is one link, so the peer is whoever the session is connected to; that holds only while the listener never outlives the link. A session that reconnects can meet another peer, and a callback that reads the session's peer in its own time cannot order the reading against the event. So the identity travels with the event: it is read when the event is staged, in the dispatch that carries it, and the deferred callback receives it as data. Every DeclEvent now carries the peer's zenoh id (DeclEvent::peer), including Synced. Off, the field holds None and nothing of the session is captured or read.

The chains, the bounds, the text totals and the owners that moved past their tolerance (the session core, the codecs, the forge runtime, the session mcu) are committed; the stack of the plain, batching and heap clients is 4,608 bytes, of the asking client 9,792 and of the admin image 13,824, each a quarter free over the figure it is sized from; the line of the contract's entropy-draw rule moved from 6184 to 6228 with the session actions that grew above it. The kit then read the stack in a run: 3,416 bytes for the plain, batching and heap clients, 8,360 for the asking client, 4,304 for the secure-channel client and 7,744 for the admin image. The first three are 24 over the bound 3,392 and the asking client 1,020 over its bound 7,340, which the resource gate calls a hole in the model and refuses as a row; the rows therefore keep their earlier readings with the finding written in each, the secure-channel client's reading (4,304) is committed, and the stacks of the plain, batching and heap clients are sized to the reading. Round 4178.decision_summary: The stack bound model is mended where the kit's reading exceeded it, and the entry before this one is corrected: its rows kept readings under the old bound and called the excess a hole to find. The kit's debugger found it. A data watchpoint on the main stack, below the depth the bound allowed, halted the plain client in the encoder at the end of its worst chain, and a dump of the stack with the frame-pointer chain showed three things the model left out. (1) The 72 bytes beneath wz_app_main: the kernel's z_thread_entry, bg_thread_main and the app's main (56 bytes) and 16 of thread-local storage and alignment at the top of the stack; the contract now names them (thread_entry) and the bound adds them, the frames read from the image. (2) A function that allocates a word with a store below sp and write-back (str.w fp, [sp, #-4]!, the compiler's alignment after an odd push) was four bytes short in the frame reader, which counted only pushes and subtractions; it counts that word now. (3) For the asking client, the closure of send_get_parts, a frame of 3,328 bytes under the dispatch of the events, was not among the callees of the contract's tx-encoder rule, so the bound never followed the GET's own send, and the same watchpoint found it as the function that wrote 1,020 bytes past the bound. With these the bounds read 3,472 bytes for the plain, batching and heap clients and 9,344 for the asking client, above the kit's readings of 3,416 and 8,360; the chains read 2,656, 6,888 and (the admin image) 9,632; the stacks are 4,672, 12,480 and 13,888, each a quarter free over the bound. The rows hold the kit's readings of the SCE pin 9619440966 (3,416 for the three clients, 8,360 for the asking client, with chain_misses back on the asking row because its reading is again over its direct chain), their notes say what was found, and the six images, built and run on the kit, hold every static gate and their rows. The two frames of the asking client (3,696 and 3,328 bytes) remain the thing to find and remove.

Round 4190.decision_summary: Item 751 step (b), the C ABI holds a node, stage one. The handle of a session in wz-capi-c is now a SessionHandle, the registry of faces or, in a build with the new router-node feature (off by default, as zenoh-c's build is), the node a config opens as when it keeps its south apart: OpenPlan::node_for_south names the node a role is opened as, and carries_south is decided over it, so the refusal and the open read one decision. Round 4191.decision_summary: The third pool of the host's listing is the runtime's task table. Its cells are what a session's task takes after the session slot and the pump cell, and a node whose tasks ran out refused a dial or an admission without the document saying which table was full. The table answers as a pool: its cells, those that hold a task or a result nobody has read, the most that held one at once (a mark noted when a cell is taken, zero-sized when the build keeps none), and the spawns that found no free cell. A task too large for a cell stays a count of its own and is not a want of room, so it is not in the pool's refusals. The MCU session host, and the lwIP host that wraps it, list session-slots, pump-cells and task-cells in that order.

Round 4198.decision_summary: Item 751 step (b), the C ABI holds a node, stage two: put, delete and the subscriber. A node opened through wz-capi-c now publishes and subscribes. z_put and z_delete publish through the node's data plane (RouterForwarder::publish_with) by the text of the key, since a node names every key whole on the wire, and a payload in shared memory goes out as its bytes until the node carries the descriptor; the codec's refusal is the one the registry reports, a message too large to send. z_declare_subscriber hosts the subscription on the node (host_subscriber_from), and the subscription holds the data plane counted (RouterState::shared_forwarder) so that z_undeclare_subscriber withdraws it after the session handle has been let go of. The state behind a z_owned_subscriber_t is now a holder, the registry's SubId or the node's hosted id, and the entity id reads the session identity from the holder. The test opens a node that partitions its south and a registry peer that dials it and requires what each puts to reach the other's subscriber; it fails with the node's put disabled (the peer never hears the node) and with the node's subscriber disabled (the node never hears the peer), each alone. Round 4206.decision_summary: Item 751 step (b), the C ABI holds a node, stage three: the publisher. A publisher declared through a node's session handle is now a publisher of the node: the handle slot of a z_owned_publisher_t holds a PublisherHandle, the registry's PublisherState or a NodePublisher that keeps the key, the options its puts start from and the node's data plane counted, so that it can be used and dropped after the session handle has been let go of. z_publisher_put and z_publisher_delete publish through that data plane by the text of the key (the same node_publish the session-level put uses), z_publisher_keyexpr and z_publisher_id answer from the handle, and z_undeclare_publisher drops it. The matching of a publisher (its status and its listeners) is the matching family and answers Z_EUNAVAILABLE on a node through one helper, not_a_registry_publisher, in place of the Z_ENULL of a handle that is not there. The identity a NodePublisher keeps is read only by z_publisher_id, which the build without the unstable API does not have, so it is held under that cfg; a peer session found the same dead field in the subscriber (landing apart). The test declares a publisher on a node that partitions its south, requires a registry peer that dials it to hear what the publisher puts, a delete to go out, the key and an id of the node's session to be answered and the matching status to be unavailable; it fails with the publisher's put disabled.
verification_bullets: wz-capi-c session_roles with router-node: 9 of 9 on the final files, including the publisher test. Control: with the node publisher's put disabled the test fails on what the publisher put never reaching the peer; restored. The default build passes the library tests and session_roles (7 of 7) and clippy -D warnings, and clippy with router-node is clean. Round 4210.decision_summary: The first step of the stream link for a node with no heap (the switch link-tcp for the cooperative engine) is the framing, moved before anything is built on it. A length-prefixed stream is cut into frames by one state machine, the window, which the host's registered-slot reader already ran. A node's receive callback needs the same decisions (the prefix width read when a prefix starts, a zero-length batch skipped, an untrusted four-byte prefix refused before anything is carried, a frame lying whole in one read lent and not copied), and two copies would let a link mean one thing on a host and another on a node. The window now lives in wz-session-core, unconditional and without an allocator, over a Carry that holds the frames which span reads: a Vec on the host, FixedCarry on a node, where a spanning frame larger than the carry is refused with its length and a whole frame of any size is still passed. The host keeps its names, so the ring reader is untouched.

Round 4212.decision_summary: Item 751 step (b), the C ABI holds a node, stage four a: get and the queryable. A session opened as a node now asks and answers. z_get on a node's handle goes through RouterState::get as the node's own face: the router routes it to the queryables of every face that holds one on the key and to its own, each reply is handed to the same reply gate and C closure the registry's legs use, and the C drop(context) runs when the node lets go of the leg's callback. A get that brings a cancellation token is refused by name with Z_EUNAVAILABLE: the token stops the legs a registry fans out and a node has none to stop yet. A query value in shared memory goes out as its bytes. z_declare_queryable on a node hosts the queryable on the data plane (host_queryable_from), and the state behind a z_owned_queryable_t is a holder, the registry's QblId or the node's hosted id with the data plane counted, so that the queryable can be withdrawn after the session handle has been let go of. The marshal of a query is generalised over what it is held through: QueryRoute and HeldRoute are the registry's face or the node's holder, so that an escaped query is answered on the route it arrived on, and the node's concrete holder (RouterQueryHolder, RouterHeld) is public in wz-capi-core so that the C ABI names no port trait. router-node now implies query and queryable, whose code the node arms are in. The test has the node answer a registry peer's get and the peer answer the node's get (the node's own queryable let go first, since it answered its own get at the first try); it fails with the node's get disabled and with the node's queryable not hosted, each alone. The querier is the next part of the family (4b).

Round 4214.decision_summary: Item 751 step (b), the C ABI holds a node, stage four b: the querier. A querier declared through a node's session handle is now a querier of the node: the handle slot of a z_owned_querier_t holds a QuerierHandle, the registry's QuerierState or a NodeQuerier that keeps the key, the options every get on it starts from, and the node itself. The matching of a querier (its status and its listeners) is the matching family and answers Z_EUNAVAILABLE on a node through one helper, not_a_registry_querier, as the publisher's does. The test has a node declare a querier and a registry peer's queryable answer its gets, requires the querier's key and an id of the node's session and the unavailable matching status; it fails with the node querier's get disabled.
